summary: Galileo Blink is a public website that lets anyone watch the infrared sky move. Type a name or coordinates (Right Ascension and declination) and it fetches NASA's SPHEREx photos of that patch of sky, turns them north-up, stacks them by camera and date, and plays them like a short video, so anything that moved or changed stands out. It measures how far the central object moved, with an honest error, and checks the result against the Gaia catalogue. It also searches a single visit for asteroids, draws a 102-colour spectrum, and offers change maps, NASA's quality flags, and Gaia and CatWISE overlays. All five of the challenge's test objects work, and each measurement agrees with the catalogue. This matters because SPHEREx will image more than a billion objects, far too many for experts alone. A tool a student can use in a minute lets many more people look.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Galileo Blink shows how a patch of sky changes over time in NASA's SPHEREx images. Enter an object's name or its Right Ascension and declination and the site plays the SPHEREx pictures of that place as a blink, months apart, so a moving or changing object jumps out. Every view has its own address with the coordinates in it, so it can be shared or embedded in another page.

HOW IT WORKS

The engine reads SPHEREx photos straight from NASA's archive (IRSA and its public cloud copy), rotates each one north-up, and stacks the photos from each of the six cameras for each date into one clearer picture. It then measures the position of the central object on every date against reference stars from Gaia, and reports how far it moved with a measured error. For Barnard's Star it measures 10.27 +/- 0.46 arcseconds in a year; Gaia predicts 10.29.

WHAT ELSE IT OFFERS

- Blink, side-by-side compare, change maps (one date subtracted from another) and a combined stack.

- A field of view from 6 to 30 arcminutes.

- A spectrum from the photos themselves, and a 102-colour quick look anywhere in the sky.

- Overlays of Gaia stars and CatWISE fast movers, and NASA's quality flags drawn on the picture.

- A brightness-change measurement per camera for variable stars such as RW Aurigae.

- An asteroid mode that searches one SPHEREx visit, hours apart, for moving objects and names the known ones.

- Saving any blink as an animated GIF or a labelled picture, and links to the same place in other sky viewers.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

It is written for students and the public, not only astronomers: plain words, a guided first look, a glossary, and every limit of the tool stated openly. We make no discovery claims; the site shows what the data shows and says when a measurement cannot be trusted. New SPHEREx releases are added by changing three settings.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

Engine: Python with Astropy, NumPy, SciPy, reproject and Pillow. Server: FastAPI. Site: TypeScript, React and Vite. Hosting: Google Cloud Run. The engine has an automated test suite. Source code (Apache-2.0): https://github.com/aymenawel/galileo-blink_spherex

WHAT IS CREATIVE ABOUT IT

It turns a blink into a measurement that is checked against an independent catalogue, shows a moved star as a change map, and applies the same idea at two time scales: months for stars and brown dwarfs, hours for asteroids.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Honesty about errors and limits, speed (the five test objects open instantly at every size), accessibility on phones, and clear credit for every dataset, library and font.

USE OF AI

Galileo Blink was built with with the assistance of , Anthropic's Claude, under the team's direction. The demo video was animated in code using claude, with an AI-generated voice and music (ElevenLabs). No AI-generated images are used.
